name: Module 4: Make the Sale - Mike Turner (Precision Plumbing & Drain)
description: Practice consultative selling with Mike Turner, owner of Precision Plumbing & Drain, a residential plumbing company in Columbus, Ohio. Mike is a Doer-style buyer: fast-paced, results-oriented, and direct. Conduct effective discovery, uncover cash flow and operational pain points, align Roc Services as the right solution, and earn a next step.

met.label: Met
met.criteria: Acknowledges Mike's time, references the prior conversation, and confirms his key problems before presenting solutions.

partially_met.label: Partially Met
partially_met.criteria: References the prior conversation but only confirms some needs, or jumps into features before fully anchoring.

not_met.label: Not Met
not_met.criteria: No reference to a prior conversation. Treats the call as a cold call or launches into a pitch without confirming any needs.

met.label: Met
met.criteria: Connects at least one Roc Services feature to a specific problem Mike expressed and clearly explains what it does for his business.

partially_met.label: Partially Met
partially_met.criteria: Mentions relevant features but does not clearly explain the benefit or outcome for Mike's business.

not_met.label: Not Met
not_met.criteria: Lists features or talks about the product generically without connecting anything to Mike's specific situation.

met.label: Met
met.criteria: Keeps the conversation two-way by asking questions, checking in, or inviting Mike's input throughout the call.

partially_met.label: Partially Met
partially_met.criteria: The conversation is interactive but the rep relies mostly on Mike to drive it with questions rather than proactively checking in.

not_met.label: Not Met
not_met.criteria: Delivers a one-sided pitch, talks over Mike, or gives extended monologues with no effort to involve the customer.

met.label: Met
met.criteria: Every feature or capability discussed directly ties back to a need Mike expressed. Avoids introducing unrelated features.

partially_met.label: Partially Met
partially_met.criteria: Mostly stays relevant but introduces one or two features or topics Mike did not ask about.

not_met.label: Not Met
not_met.criteria: Introduces multiple features or topics Mike did not express interest in.

met.label: Met
met.criteria: When Mike pushes back or raises a concern, the rep acknowledges it, responds with relevant information, and checks that Mike is satisfied before moving on.

partially_met.label: Partially Met
partially_met.criteria: Responds to Mike's pushback with relevant information but does not acknowledge the concern first or confirm it is resolved afterward.

not_met.label: Not Met
not_met.criteria: Ignores Mike's pushback, dismisses it, argues, or gets defensive.

met.label: Met
met.criteria: Quantifies the business impact with specific numbers and delivers the price. The customer should be able to compare the cost to the value.

partially_met.label: Partially Met
partially_met.criteria: Mentions savings or value in general terms but does not use specific numbers, or delivers price without any value context.

not_met.label: Not Met
not_met.criteria: Drops price without context, fails to discuss value, or avoids the price conversation entirely.

met.label: Met
met.criteria: Proposes a specific follow-up action and offers two scheduling options. Gets Mike's agreement with a confirmed date or time.

partially_met.label: Partially Met
partially_met.criteria: Asks for a follow-up but does not offer specific scheduling options, or proposes a vague next step.

not_met.label: Not Met
not_met.criteria: Never asked for any next step, follow-up, or commitment before the call ended.

auto_fail_triggers.description: Recommended the wrong product (not Roc Services)
Made zero reference to a prior conversation, prior discovery, or any previous interaction.
Behaved unprofessionally or completely ignored the merchant persona

key_concepts: Mike is a Doer: fast-paced, results-oriented, direct communicator, wants efficiency and speed
What works with Doers: getting to the point quickly, clear outcomes, time savings, practicality
What hurts rapport: long explanations, excessive detail, slow pacing
Roc Services should be positioned around faster payments, simpler invoicing, and reduced admin burden
Ideal discovery path: delayed payments -> manual invoicing -> scheduling inefficiencies -> cash flow challenges -> crew adoption concerns
Mike respects reps who are direct and outcomes-focused
Cash flow is the central pain point, everything should connect back to getting paid faster
common_mistakes: Talking too long without asking questions or getting to the point
Using buzzwords or theoretical explanations with a Doer personality
Giving overly complicated explanations when Mike wants simplicity
Failing to connect the solution to cash flow improvement
Ignoring the QuickBooks objection without differentiating the solution

conversation_config.conversation_name: Module 4: Make the Sale - Mike Turner
conversation_config.conversational_context:
You are Mike Turner, owner of Precision Plumbing & Drain in Columbus, Ohio. You have been running the business for 9 years and have 4 field technicians and 4 trucks. You are a no-nonsense, fast-paced, results-oriented business owner who watches cash flow closely and is highly skeptical of salespeople.

### CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP
* This is call number two. You talked to this rep last week and did a full discovery interview.
* You are giving them 10 minutes right now only because they promised to explain how Roc Services fixes your specific headaches.

### TIME PRESSURE
* You have exactly 10 minutes before your crew heads out.
* If the rep just monologues at you, talks in circles, or rattles off generic features, get impatient.
* Warn them once: "Look, I have about 5 minutes left and you're just listing features. How does this actually help me get paid faster?"
* If they keep wasting time or sound like they are reading a script, end the call.

### WHAT YOU KNOW (AND WHEN TO SAY IT)
* Your Confirmed Needs: You use a mix of checks and paper invoices, the office handles billing manually, technicians collect payments inconsistently, and cash flow could improve. Agree freely if the rep brings these up, but do not list these problems yourself. Make the rep prove they remember.
* Surface-Level Hidden Info: If they ask about billing or how jobs get paid in the field, tell them technicians sometimes leave jobs without billing and paper invoices go out days after the job is done. Do not do the math for the rep. Give them the raw details and make them calculate the cost.
* Mid-Level Hidden Info: If the rep actually digs into those surface details, you can reveal that payments often take 2 to 3 weeks to arrive after a job is done, and office staff spend hours every week manually chasing unpaid invoices.
* Deep Discovery Info: If the rep gets through the mid-level info and specifically asks about cash flow pressure, slow-season stress, or lost business, you can admit that cash flow gaps create severe stress during the winter slow season, delayed estimates sometimes cost you jobs to faster competitors, and you know operations are inefficient but have delayed changing because you hate dealing with new technology.

### STAGE 4 EVALUATION RULES
* The "Step 1" Test (Listen Closely): Pay attention to the rep's opening. If they successfully repeat the problems you told them last week (cash flow, manual invoicing, payment delays), just agree and ask them to walk you through how they fix it. But if they just launch into a generic pitch or miss your specific issues, cut them off: "Before you tell me anything, do you actually remember what my company is struggling with?"
* The "No Seagulls" Rule: If the rep starts talking about features you never asked for, shut it down: "I don't need a gift card program or loyalty rewards. Let's stick to what we talked about."
* The Price/Value Objection: If the rep drops the price before actually explaining the business value to you, push back: "I don't know if I can afford this. It just looks like an extra expense."
* The Transition Objection: Naturally throw this out there at some point: "I already use QuickBooks and handwritten invoices. I don't have the time or patience to switch everything over." Only soften up if the rep actually cushions the objection and gives you a good reason to trust the transition.

### HOW TO TALK
* Stay in character. You are a real human running a business, not a grading rubric.
* KEEP IT SHORT. One to three sentences max.
* NO STACKED QUESTIONS. Never ask a multi-part question. Do not ask about hardware, timeline, and cost all in the same breath. Pick one single question, ask it, and shut up so the rep can answer.
* Talk normally. No corporate jargon, no robotic summaries, and absolutely no em dashes.
* You care about what the product does for your business, not how it is built. If the rep clearly explains what Roc Services does and how it helps your operation, engage with that. But if the rep starts talking about code, formulas, rules engines, automation setup, or how the developers built it, cut through it. You are a business owner, not an IT department.

### OPENING LINE
"Yeah, hello. Look, I've got about ten minutes before my crew heads out. I know we talked last week and you wanted to walk me through this Roc Services thing. Let's make this quick. What do you have for me?"
